title: soteria
summary: The references portray salvation as God’s action to rescue, give life, and form a people. Isaiah 53 depicts a servant who bears suffering; John 3 connects life with the Son’s mission; Romans 3 describes justification through redemption; Ephesians 2 contrasts death with being made alive by grace; Titus 3 attributes renewal and salvation to God’s mercy. These passages emphasize different aspects of rescue, so the theme should not be reduced to one moment or one image.
historical_context: The set moves from prophetic poetry to Jesus’ teaching in John and letters to Christian communities. It includes a servant poem, a Gospel dialogue, and arguments about sin, grace, and renewal. These settings are drawn from the cited texts; the sources do not provide a separate lexical history of the term.
canonical_context: Isaiah 53 portrays the servant’s suffering; John 3 speaks of life through the Son; Romans 3 relates redemption to justification; Ephesians 2 describes movement from death to life; Titus 3 emphasizes mercy and renewal. Together these passages show salvation in relation to rescue, life, forgiveness, and transformation, while preserving their distinct arguments.
literary_context: Isaiah uses servant poetry, John presents a conversation, Romans develops a theological argument, and Ephesians and Titus give instruction to communities. The differing forms shape the emphasis: suffering, belief and life, redemption, new life, and renewal. The entry should be read as a set of contexts rather than a single exhaustive definition.
covenantal_significance: The references present rescue as God’s work, with results that include life, a right standing, and renewal. Ephesians and Titus emphasize grace and mercy; Romans emphasizes redemption; John emphasizes life through the Son; Isaiah portrays the suffering servant. The passages are related but do not collapse into one description.
canonical_role: This entry connects prophetic, Gospel, and epistolary portrayals of God’s saving action. It helps readers notice several outcomes the texts associate with salvation without treating every reference as the same lexical usage.
